verses.note: Fire and smoke are the signs of God's presence throughout the Old Testament. Abram sees, in a sleep of terror, a small form of what Israel will see at Sinai.

Joseph has the one opportunity of his life to impress Pharaoh, and he begins by denying his own ability and directing the king's attention to God. His later authority rests on that refusal to take the credit that belongs to God.

Moses asked to see God's glory (33:18) and was answered with a proclamation of God's goodness and name. In this chapter God's glory is revealed chiefly as his character, heard more than seen, which is the pattern John's Gospel follows when it speaks of glory ‘full of grace and truth’ (John 1:14).

God's glory changes the one who is near it. Moses reflects light he does not generate and does not notice, a picture the New Testament takes up for the transformation of believers who behold the Lord (2 Corinthians 3:18) and sees fulfilled in the transfigured Christ (Matthew 17:2).

God's concern for his name is not vanity; his name is his revealed character, and the nations' knowledge of the true God depends on it. Isaiah 48:9-11 and Psalm 106:8 make the same point. Because God's glory is the motive, his grace rests on something steadier than the recipients' worth.
